May. Costel is driving the lorry to Portugal, with a stop in Madrid. Andrei has come with him as co-driver, to photograph the journey. In the trailer, among the pallets of goods, are four boxes holding a hundred copies of the Romanian edition. They’re somewhere in northern Italy.
Costel, how many kilometres to Madrid?
About fifteen hundred. The motorway we’re on now goes as far as Nice, where we’ll make our next stop.
And when will we see Señor Andrés?
The man we’re going to see is expecting us on the twenty-eighth. Marta says it’s the day he’s at his best, because her mother will be with him.
Do you know what worries me most? That there’ll be a strike in France, like you said.
I’ve talked to a French colleague whose brother works at the border. He says there’s no problem, which is good news.
My dad asked me to take photos of everything we see. He says it’s the trip the club will talk about most.
Your dad is a man you couldn’t talk to before. Now he never stops talking.
Thanks to Ecaterina. She’s the person we all owe the most to.
And the person for whom I’m driving fifteen hundred kilometres with a hundred books I can’t read properly. Put some music on, go on. And find a rest area where they sell decent coffee.
Pronounced as a single word: [el-KUAL], [la-KUAL]. “Cual” has one syllable.
KU-yo: the “y” is a glide, like the “y” in “yes”.
The part between commas is said faster and in a lower tone, like a parenthesis: «Costel, que conduce el camión, es de Bucarest».
1. Que, quien, el que after prepositions
El hombre al que vamos a ver. / El hombre a quien vamos a ver.
La autopista por la que vamos.
El viaje del que se va a hablar.

A typical mistake: the preposition is left at the end or disappears. «La persona que hablé» ✗ → «La persona con la que hablé» / «con quien hablé» ✓. In Spanish the preposition goes BEFORE the relative, and the article agrees with the antecedent.
“Quien / quienes” is used only for people and usually after a preposition or in non-defining clauses: «la persona con quien hablé», «Costel, quien conduce…».
2. El cual, la cual: the formal register
“El cual / la cual / los cuales / las cuales” mean the same as “el que” but are more formal. They are required after long or compound prepositions:
She’s the person thanks to whom we met.
The fair, during which the book will be presented, starts on the twenty-eighth.
There’s a sign, above which hangs a lamp.
“Cuyo” expresses possession and agrees with the thing possessed (what follows), NOT with the possessor:
un compañero cuyo hermano trabaja en la frontera
una librería cuya puerta era verde
Marta, cuyas novelas se venden mucho
In informal speech some Spaniards avoid “cuyo” and say «un compañero que su hermano…» ✗. That’s wrong; in the exam use “cuyo”.
What worries me most is the strike. (lo que = what, at the start)
Take photos of everything you see.
He says there’s no problem, which is good news. (lo cual = refers to the whole preceding clause)
“Lo cual” always comes after a comma and picks up a whole idea. “Lo que” can also come at the start. After a comma both are possible: «…, lo que / lo cual es una buena noticia».
Los libros que están en la caja son para la feria.
only the ones in the box
Los libros, que están en la caja, son para la feria.
all the books (and by the way, they’re in the box)

Busca un área donde vendan café decente.
I don’t know whether it exists

Un autor que sus libros leí.

Busca un área donde venden café bueno.

La Feria del Libro de Madrid
An informative text about the Madrid Book Fair, full of relative clauses. Notice the pronouns and their agreement.
The Madrid Book Fair, which has been held every year since 1933, is one of the most important cultural events in Spain. It takes place in the Retiro park, where hundreds of wooden stands are set up.
In each stand there is a bookshop or a publisher, whose booksellers recommend new titles to visitors. The authors, for whom readers sometimes wait for hours, sign copies in the afternoons.
What surprises foreigners most is the atmosphere: whole families stroll among the stands, which turns the fair into a big popular festival.
Each year the fair invites a country, thanks to which Madrid people discover authors they didn’t know. Visitors looking for rare books usually go early, when there are fewer people.
¿Desde cuándo se celebra la Feria del Libro de Madrid?
¿Qué hacen los visitantes que buscan libros raros?

Costel’s lorry left Bucharest one Thursday in May, at five in the morning, with forty pallets of car parts for a customer in Porto and, at the back of the trailer, tightly tied down, four cardboard boxes holding a hundred copies of a blue book. In the cab, besides Costel, was Andrei, with his camera, a backpack and a list of instructions written by his father, Domnul Dan, whose handwriting was so small you needed a magnifying glass to read it.

In spite of the hour, there were people seeing them off in the company car park. Ana had come with Rosa Elena, who was carrying a parcel wrapped in newspaper: a new drawing for Señor Andrés, showing a huge lorry loaded with books, with a smiling driver and a co-driver taking photos. Domnul Dan, Andrei’s father, had come too, with a thermos of coffee and some sandwiches made by his wife. He gave his son a long, awkward hug, the first in many years.

The first instruction said: “Obey Costel in everything, except in matters of food.” The second: “Call your mother every night.” The third, underlined twice: “Take photos of everything you see, because this is something we’ll remember all our lives.” Andrei read the list aloud. Costel laughed so hard that he nearly missed the motorway exit.

They crossed the Hungarian border in mid-morning. At the first rest area, Costel introduced Andrei to an enormous man with a moustache, wearing the shirt of a Budapest football team. It was Zoltán, the Hungarian lorry driver with whom he had watched the video call with Andrés in December, both of them in the cab, crying like children. Zoltán had followed the story on his phone ever since, thanks to the translations Costel did for him with great patience and very little vocabulary.

When Zoltán saw the boxes of books, he asked permission to touch one. He took it out carefully, opened it and looked at the first page without understanding a thing, because he knew neither Romanian nor Spanish. Then he said something in Hungarian to Costel, who translated as best he could: that his grandmother had had a sweetheart in Vienna before the war, of whom she had never heard again, and that he had always wondered what had happened. Costel gave him a copy. Zoltán put it in his cab, next to the photo of his wife.

In Austria, in the middle of a storm, their windscreen wiper broke. Costel stopped in a mountain village whose only garage was closed because it was Sunday. He knocked on the door of the house next door, which belonged to the mechanic. A man in pyjamas opened it who, to their great surprise, turned out to be Romanian, from a village in Maramureș. He changed the part in twenty minutes, wouldn’t take any money and, in return, only asked them to leave a blue book for his mother, who lived with him and missed reading in her own language.

They crossed Austria in the rain and northern Italy under a sun that made the Alps shine as if they were made of glass. Andrei took hundreds of photos: mountains, tunnels, service areas, sleeping lorry drivers, a village whose bell tower had a stork on top, and above all Costel, driving with both hands on the wheel and singing Romanian songs from the eighties, whose lyrics he knew by heart but whose tunes he made up.

At night they slept in the cab, Costel in the lower bunk and Andrei in the upper one. Before going to sleep they talked. Andrei discovered that Costel, whom he had always seen as a cheerful man, had spent very lonely years on the road after his daughter went to Valencia. Costel discovered that Andrei, whom he had always seen as a shy boy, had wanted to be a photographer since he was ten and had never dared to tell his father, which, according to him, was no longer necessary, because his father had guessed on his own.

Every night, as he had promised, Andrei called his mother. And every night, without having promised, Costel called Ecaterina, who always asked the same question: whether the boxes were properly tied down. Costel answered that they were, that they were safer than the gold in a Swiss bank, and described to her the landscape they had seen that day. Ecaterina listened in silence. One night she confessed she had never made that journey overland, and that she liked imagining it through the eyes of a lorry driver.

They reached Nice at night. Costel parked in a rest area from which you could see the sea, lit by the moon. Andrei, who had never seen the Mediterranean, stood looking at it for a long time without saying anything. Costel told him that the first time he saw it, thirty years ago, he had been speechless too, and that even today, every time he passed by, he stopped for five minutes, even if it was the middle of the night, even if he was running late. “There are things for which it’s worth losing five minutes,” he said.

At the French border, against all expectations, there was no strike. The brother of Costel’s French colleague, who worked at the checkpoint, waved them through without opening the trailer. Costel decided it was a sign. Andrei decided it was simply luck. They argued about it all the way to Montpellier, where they stopped to eat at a roadside restaurant whose owner, seeing the Romanian number plate, served them a double portion of chips.

They entered Spain at La Junquera on the twenty-seventh, at sunset. Costel stopped the lorry at the first Spanish service area, got out, knelt down and touched the ground with his hand, the way the Pope did on the news. Andrei took a photo of him. Costel told him not to show it to anyone, which, naturally, was the first thing Andrei did: he sent it to the whole club, which greeted it with forty laughing messages in less than a minute.

They reached Madrid the next day, at noon. Costel left the lorry in a heavy-vehicle car park on the outskirts, because an eighteen-wheeler wouldn’t fit in the streets of the Barrio de las Letras, and they loaded the four boxes into a taxi whose driver, a man from Toledo, offered to help when he found out what they were for. “I read the story in the paper,” he said. “My wife cried for two days.” He wouldn’t take any money for the fare.

Marta was waiting for them at the door of the building on the calle del Prado. They carried the boxes up the stairs, which took them half an hour and a lot of sweat, because each box weighed twenty-five kilos and the building had no lift. In the hallway, Costel stopped in front of the bookshop’s green sign. He looked at it for a long time. He said it was smaller than he had imagined. And more beautiful, too.

Andrés was in his armchair by the window, with the blanket over his legs. Pilar, who had come from Seville for the fair, was sitting beside him. Marta introduced them: “Grandpa, this is Costel, the lorry driver I told you about. And this is Andrei, the photographer.” Andrés looked Costel up and down, very carefully, the way he used to look at new customers in the bookshop. Then he asked, in his weak voice:
“Are you the lorry driver who was crying in Hungary?”

Costel froze. He went red to the tips of his ears. He looked at Marta, who was covering her mouth so as not to laugh. And then, with great dignity, he answered that yes, it was him, but that the one who had really cried the most was his Hungarian friend, Zoltán, who, by the way, sent his regards. Andrés burst out laughing. It was a long laugh, the kind Marta hadn’t heard for months.

Costel opened one of the boxes and took out a copy. He gave it to Andrés with both hands, the way you hand over something very fragile. Andrés took it, held it for a moment on his open left hand, like a tray, and opened it at the first page. He read the two dedications, his granddaughter’s and Ecaterina’s. He didn’t understand Romanian, but he didn’t need to. He ran his finger over the words of the second one: “Pentru A., care a așteptat.”
“What does it say here?” he asked.

Costel translated, slowly, in his lorry driver’s Spanish: “Para A., que esperó.” Andrés nodded. He closed the book. He put it on his knees, on top of Rayuela, so that the two books lay one on top of the other, the old and the new, the one from 1963 and the one from this year. Then he looked out of the window and said, to no one in particular: “Tomorrow she’s coming. The woman I waited for.” And he fell asleep.

That night, Costel and Andrei slept on Marta’s sofa bed, because Costel refused to leave the books alone. Before going to sleep, Andrei showed Costel the photos of the journey on the camera screen: more than a thousand. They went through them one by one, in silence. The last one showed Andrés asleep in his armchair, with the two books on his knees. Costel asked him to send it to him. That night he made it his phone wallpaper, instead of the photo of the lorry.

The next day, at eleven in the morning, a plane from Bucharest would land at Barajas. On board would be Ana, Mihai, Rosa Elena and an eighty-year-old translator carrying in her bag a magnifying glass, a notebook full of crossings-out and a frying pan that a Romanian doctor had insisted on bringing just in case. But that’s another story, which we’ll tell in the next chapter.
